fieldMarks: Slender, cylindrical snake 1.5-3 ft long with red, black and white bands; red bands always bordered by black on both sides (WDFW; ADW).
Top of the head black, chin and throat often white, and the first band behind the head is white (ADW).
Red bands may be broken into wedges or reduced or absent, especially in Sierra Nevada populations (ADW).
behavior: Mainly diurnal, but may be nocturnal in hot weather (NatureServe; WDFW).
Searches under surface objects for lizards, small snakes and bird eggs; also eats mammals, and juveniles mainly eat lizards (NatureServe).
Mating April-May, eggs laid June-July, 2-9 per clutch (NatureServe).
Found under woody debris and rocks; inactive in cold and extreme heat (WDFW; NatureServe).
habitat: Moist open coniferous forest, oak woodland, riparian woodland, chaparral, coastal sage scrub and open woodland with rocks or rotting logs, often near streams; sea level to about 2,750 m (NatureServe).
range: Western United States: around the Central Valley of California along the Sierra Nevada and Northern Coast Ranges, north into the Klamath Mountains in Oregon, with a disjunct population in the Columbia Gorge in Washington; populations south of Monterey Bay are treated as L. multifasciata by NatureServe (NatureServe).

lookalikes.name: Coral snakes
lookalikes.howToTell: Harmless and superficially resembles a coral snake; its red bands are bordered by black (WDFW).

lookalikes.name: California kingsnake
lookalikes.howToTell: Mountain kingsnake has red, black and white bands with red bordered by black (WDFW, ADW); California kingsnake is black and white or brown and cream, banded or striped (NPS Cabrillo).
